idiom_name: synchronized + wait()/notifyAll() on the JVM monitor
implementation_notes: Scala runs on the JVM, so the intrinsic monitor is available unchanged: this.synchronized { while (!predicate) wait() } with notifyAll from the mutating side is the classic guarded suspension, and scala.concurrent supplies only blocking helpers (blocking { ... } informs the ForkJoinPool that a thread is parked) rather than a condition abstraction. The futures documentation discourages blocking inside futures, which is a reason to prefer java.util.concurrent queues or a Promise-based shape in asynchronous code; keep the monitor form for short, thread-affine guards and for code that must not depend on a concurrency library.
pitfalls: Blocking inside a Future starves the global ForkJoinPool unless the wait is wrapped in scala.concurrent.blocking.
wait/notifyAll outside a synchronized block throw IllegalMonitorStateException, and the whole wait set must share one monitor.
Scala's synchronized is reentrant, so calling a guarded method from another guarded method on the same object re-enters the monitor and can deadlock on a nested wait.

variants.name: java.util.concurrent blocking queue
variants.implementation_notes: java.util.concurrent gives Scala the same library guard as Java: take() waits for an item and put() waits for space on a bounded queue, with timed poll/offer variants and an explicit happens-before edge, and scala.concurrent.Promise/Future express the wait for one result rather than for shared state. Choose the queue form whenever the guard is items-or-space available, and keep the monitor form for guards over state that is not a queue.
variants.code_sketch:
import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue

val q = new LinkedBlockingQueue[Int](64)   // bounded: put() gets a guard too

val consumer = new Thread(() =>
  while (true) println(q.take())           // blocks while the queue is empty
)
consumer.start()

q.put(42)                                   // blocks while the queue is full
pitfalls: poll(timeout) returns null on timeout, which collides with null elements: never enqueue null and check the result explicitly.
An unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue silently drops the 'space available' half of the guard; bound it when backpressure matters.
